transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2027-03-22 09:00 PT
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Attendees: Lena Martin (Redwood AE), Omar Reyes (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (VP Eng, Silverpine), Tom Becker (Cloud Architect), Rachel Kim (Security Lead), Ethan Lo (SRE)

Summary:
Priya and her team run an analytics platform that enriches customer events with embeddings and runs on a hybrid architecture: primary workloads in AWS us-east-1, heavy edge ingestion in three regional PoPs (eu-west-1, ap-northeast-1, us-west-2). Their primary asks: private connectivity for sensitive PII-enriched payloads (no internet egress), region gating (data residency), and predictable latency guarantees. Exploring Redwood Private with VPC peering or Transit Gateway + Private Endpoints. They want a checklist, security docs, and a technical deep dive on actual network designs and perf expectations.

Topics covered:
- High-level architecture and constraints
- Private deployment options (VPC peering, Transit Gateway, PrivateLink / Private Endpoints)
- Region constraints and data residency gating
- Egress controls, IP planning, and NAT/firewall needs
- Auth/KMS/SSO questions: KMS wrapped keys, HSM, SAML SSO, audit logs
- Latency targets and fallback policies (hosted -> dedicated -> private)

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena Martin: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh I'm Lena from Redwood, with Omar and Maya on the call from our SE team. How are you Priya?
[00:10] Priya Shah: Good thanks, excited to dig in, we got a bunch of network questions, and Rachel will lead the security parts.
[00:15] Tom Becker: Hi all, quick background - we run most compute in us-east-1, but we have edge collectors in three regions that must not egress to public internet. We're evaluating Private deployment for that.
[00:30] Omar Reyes: Great, thanks Tom. Just to confirm, key constraints are: no internet egress for PII traffic, ability to restrict by region, and predictable p99 latency under 200ms for inference?
[00:40] Priya Shah: Correct, p99 under 200ms in-region is goal for the user-facing flows. For batch scoring non-critical.
[00:52] Rachel Kim: And SOC2/ISO compliance is a hard ask — need audit logs, SSO integrations, and customer-managed KMS/HSM option.
[01:05] Maya Chen: Totally, we support SAML SSO, RBAC, audit logs. For KMS you can bring-your-own via KMS integrations, and we support HSM-backed key stores in Private.
[01:20] Ethan Lo: Are there additional egress IPs we need to allow? We prefer to firewall to explicit endpoints only.
[01:30] Lena Martin: For Private we'll provide private endpoints inside your VPC or peered VPCs — no public IPs required. There are egress rules only if you opt into outbound patches or telemetry to a Redwood control plane; otherwise full air gap is possible with on-prem package.
[01:45] Tom Becker: Can you walk through peering vs Transit Gateway? Our network team generally standardizes on TGW for multiple VPCs across accounts and regions.
[02:00] Omar Reyes: Sure. Peering is point-to-point and easier for single VPC pairings. Transit Gateway scales better for many VPCs/accounts and supports central route table control. For high scale hybrid we typically recommend TGW + AWS PrivateLink for endpoints — TGW handles routing between region hubs, while PrivateLink gives you interface endpoints into the Redwood service.
[02:30] Priya Shah: So PrivateLink means the traffic terminates on an ENI in our VPC?
[02:35] Maya Chen: Exactly — it gives you an ENI-based interface endpoint and eliminates traversing public internet. There are some cross-account IAM and endpoint service setup steps.
[02:45] Rachel Kim: How does this work for multi-region? Do you deploy separate Private stacks in each region?
[02:55] Omar Reyes: We offer Private control planes that can be regional. For strict residency you can pin a model serving cluster to a specific region. In practice customers either deploy a regional Private for eu/APAC or use hub-and-spoke with TGW to keep traffic in-region where required. We'll share an architecture doc with patterns.
[03:25] Tom Becker: Any limitations on peering with our on-prem via Direct Connect? We have a DX+TGW topology.
[03:35] Lena Martin: Direct Connect + TGW is supported. The common pattern: on-prem -> DX -> TGW -> regional Redwood VPCs (or peered VPCs) with PrivateLink endpoints. You maintain full control on your side.
[03:50] Ethan Lo: Are there any extra IP ranges or route table constraints imposed by Redwood? We want to avoid overlapping CIDRs.
[04:00] Maya Chen: We recommend non-overlapping /16 or /20 ranges depending on scale. We'll share a suggested IP planning spreadsheet. Overlaps require NAT or asymmetric routing workarounds which are painful.
[04:20] Priya Shah: What about latency? Any example numbers for p50/p95/p99 in-region with Private deployment?
[04:30] Omar Reyes: Rough ballparks: p50 ~ 15-30ms, p95 ~ 60-100ms, p99 depends on sequence length and model size — for typical 2k token LLMs it's around 120-220ms in-region on dedicated GPU pools. For highest certainty we run a short benchmark; I'll prepare numbers for your expected qps.
[05:05] Tom Becker: That p99 range is big — what's the primary cause?
[05:10] Omar Reyes: Two things: model KV cache warmup and network tail when traffic goes cross-az or crosses to a different region. Caching mitigates much of the token-level latency. Also larger models or longer context inflate decode time.
[05:30] Priya Shah: For sensitive payloads we'd like guaranteed zone-local paths. Is that possible?
[05:35] Maya Chen: Yes, you can pin workloads to AZs and we can present endpoints in the same AZ where we have capacity. It does reduce autoscaling flexibility but helps latency and compliance.
[05:55] Rachel Kim: KMS question again — can we hold keys in our KMS and have Redwood use KMS decrypt at runtime, or do keys need to be uploaded?
[06:05] Omar Reyes: You can bring-your-own KMS; Redwood integrates with cloud KMS (AWS KMS) roles. For full HSM we support integrating with HSM-backed stores in Private deployments. We do not require uploading plain-text keys.
[06:25] Tom Becker: What about logging and audit trails? Need to show chain of custody on requests.
[06:35] Maya Chen: Audit logs include per-request traces and token counts; logs can be streamed to your S3 or delivered to a SIEM via our connectors. For Private we can also enable extended retention in your own logging backend.
[06:55] Ethan Lo: Do you have documented latency for PrivateLink interface endpoints? We're concerned about additional hops.
[07:05] Omar Reyes: PrivateLink does add a small interface latency — typically single-digit ms in-region — but avoids public routing. The bigger contributor is cross-region transit.
[07:20] Priya Shah: Are there any ports/protocols we need to open for NAT or health checks?
[07:25] Lena Martin: Health checks use standard HTTPS (443) to the private endpoints. For control plane telemetry there may be egress to specific vendor endpoints unless you opt into isolated mode.
[07:40] Tom Becker: Can Redwood run inside our VPC as a full on-prem deploy (air-gapped)? We're evaluating airgap for the most restricted workloads.
[07:50] Maya Chen: We have an on-prem package — full control plane in your environment, no external control plane required. That path is heavier operationally but gives maximum isolation.
[08:05] Rachel Kim: Do you offer certificate rotation automation and integration with our internal PKI?
[08:10] Omar Reyes: Yes, cert management can be integrated; we support certs issued by your internal CA and automated rotation tooling for the service certs.
[08:25] Priya Shah: One of our major gating questions is cost tradeoff: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Can you summarize quickly?
[08:35] Lena Martin: Hosted is fastest to onboard and lowest operational burden but doesn't meet air-gap/no-egress requirements. Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and cost efficiency at scale. Private (VPC/autonomous) is highest control and compliance but requires more ops and often higher TCO. We'll include a comparative spreadsheet.
[09:00] Tom Becker: For Dedicated vs Private, are the kernels/serving runtime identical? We want predictability.
[09:10] Maya Chen: Yes, the runtime is the same stack; differences are in networking and control plane placement. You get identical model behavior and can pin versions.
[09:25] Ethan Lo: Regarding region gating: if we route EU traffic to a regional Redwood cluster, how do you ensure data doesn't leave region for logs/metrics?
[09:35] Omar Reyes: We can configure log sinks to terminate to your regional S3 and region-bound monitoring. Control plane telemetry can be restricted; for strict residency we recommend regional Private instances.
[09:55] Priya Shah: Ok let's talk specific topology. I'll hand over to Tom to share the current VPC layout.
[10:02] Tom Becker: (shares screen) We have account A: hub/TGW in us-east-1 with spoke VPCs in us-west-2 and eu-west-1 and Direct Connect to colo. CIDRs: 10.10.0.0/16 (hub), 10.20.0.0/16 (us-west), 10.30.0.0/16 (eu-west). We prefer to keep Redwood endpoints in separate peered account to limit blast radius.
[10:40] Maya Chen: Sounds good. Common pattern is a separate Redwood VPC per region, peered to the hub or attached to TGW. Use interface endpoints for private connectivity and security groups to restrict egress.
[11:05] Tom Becker: How do you approach IP management when Redwood VPC is in our account vs Redwood-managed account?
[11:15] Lena Martin: If deployed in your account you control the CIDRs. If Redwood deploys in our managed account we provide our recommended ranges and will coordinate to avoid overlaps. Many customers prefer deploying Redwood stack into a management account to keep infra ops minimal.
[11:35] Rachel Kim: For compliance, can we get a SOC2 + penetration test report as part of the evaluation?
[11:40] Lena Martin: Yes, we will share the SOC2 report and recent pen test summary; full artifacts can be shared under NDA.
[11:50] Priya Shah: On data in transit: do you support enforcing TLS mutual auth between our services and Redwood endpoints?
[11:58] Omar Reyes: We support mTLS for Private and can integrate with your CA for cert issuance.
[12:10] Ethan Lo: What's the operational model for patching, upgrades for Private? We need maintenance windows.
[12:20] Maya Chen: For Private you control maintenance windows in on-prem installs; for Redwood-hosted Private we coordinate and provide maintenance windows and options for staged upgrades.
[12:35] Tom Becker: For discovery, what artifacts should we expect from Redwood?
[12:40] Lena Martin: We'll send a VPC peering checklist, Transit Gateway reference architecture diagram, an IP planning spreadsheet, SOC2/security pack link, and a short benchmark plan.
[12:51] Priya Shah: Also, can you show sample Terraform modules or CloudFormation for setting up PrivateLink and the endpoint service?
[12:58] Omar Reyes: Yes we have TF modules and example templates; will attach links.
[13:05] Tom Becker: Any gotchas with inter-account PrivateLink?
[13:10] Maya Chen: You need to accept the endpoint service in the service consumer account and configure security groups carefully; also ensure cross-account permissions for acceptance. We'll document that.
[13:25] Rachel Kim: Regarding retention, how long do you keep request metadata by default and can we override?
[13:35] Omar Reyes: Defaults are 30 days for metadata but for Private you can configure retention and store logs in your own S3 for unlimited retention.
[13:50] Ethan Lo: One more thing on bandwidth: if we have heavy real-time ingestion, does Redwood recommend burst capacity or reserved lanes?
[13:58] Lena Martin: For high sustained throughput we recommend Dedicated reserved capacity; for variable spikes we can provision burst capacity. We'll include capacity sizing questions in the checklist.
[14:15] Priya Shah: Ok this is helpful. Quick follow-up: can Redwood's runtime run on our on-prem GPU boxes if we give you the images?
[14:25] Maya Chen: The on-prem package supports deployments to customer-managed GPU clusters with some validation. We'll need to check exact driver/kernel versions and deliver a compatibility matrix.
[14:40] Tom Becker: Are there limitations for cross-region replication of KV cache? We want fast failover without cold-starts.
[14:50] Omar Reyes: KV cache is local to serving nodes; we support warm standby patterns and synchronous replication is expensive. Typical approach is regional warm standby and prefix caching; we'll discuss specifics in the deep dive.
[15:05] Priya Shah: Thanks. Can you email the checklist and schedule the deep dive for next week?
[15:12] Lena Martin: Absolutely, we'll send the VPC peering checklist and propose times for the week of 2027-03-29.
[15:20] Tom Becker: Great. Anything else from Redwood?
[15:25] Omar Reyes: I'll prepare a short perf baseline and include p50/p95/p99 for your expected payloads.
[15:30] Rachel Kim: We'll share any compliance docs and the list of internal reviewers.
[15:35] Lena Martin: Perfect, recap then next steps: we (1) send checklist & security pack, (2) Omar sends perf baseline + TF examples, (3) schedule deep technical session, (4) Tom shares VPC layout + region restrictions. We'll follow-up via email and attach the deck.
[15:55] Priya Shah: Thanks all.
